h1: Comet hops and the wild grapefruit note of an old variety
title: Comet Hops: Wild Grapefruit Note | Craft Beer School
desc: Comet is an old American hop with a wild grapefruit note that is back in fashion. What it tastes like and a simple single hop pale ale for a home brewer.
teaser: A hop that was nearly forgotten and now smells of wild grapefruit. Comet is an acquired taste.
standfirst: Comet is an old American variety with a grapefruit and grassy character. It lost favour, then came back when brewers wanted something different. Here is how to try it at home.
sections: An old hop with a wild streak

Comet is an American hop bred by the United States Department of Agriculture and released in the 1970s. A wild American hop is in its ancestry. That explains its odd character. After years in the shade it came back in recent years, when craft brewers started hunting for flavours beyond Cascade.

Alpha acids sit roughly in the 8 to 11% range, which makes it useful for both bittering and aroma. Most people use it late. Dose it modestly the first time.

Expect grapefruit, grapefruit pith and a wild, grassy note that some tasters call catty. The aroma is bold and sharp rather than juicy. It is not a soft, sweet fruit hop. It is closer to the pith of the fruit than the flesh. Think of the bitter white layer under the skin, not the juice.

That edge is the appeal. In a pale ale or IPA with a dry finish it feels fresh and a little untamed. In a sweet, round beer it can clash. If you find it too much, pair it with a softer hop such as Sabro or Talus.
A single hop pale ale for 20 litres

Use 4 kg of pale malt and 200 g of light crystal. Before you brew, try the hop on its own. Steep a gram of pellets in 100 mL of hot water in a covered glass, let it cool and smell it. This hop tea shows the raw grapefruit and grass in a minute and tells you whether you want to spend 20 L of wort on it. Mash at 66 °C for 60 minutes. That gives a dry finish, which suits a sharp hop. Add 25 g of Comet at the start of the boil. At 10% alpha and 25% utilisation in 20 L, that gives about 31 IBU (25 g x 0.10 x 0.25 x 1,000 / 20 L).

Add 30 g at 5 minutes and 40 g in a whirlpool at 80 °C for 20 minutes. Ferment with a clean American ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. Dry hop with 40 g for three days at the end of fermentation. Taste before bottling and again at two weeks.

Chill the wort quickly. A slow cool-down after the whirlpool lets the oils boil off and invites DMS (a cooked sweetcorn off flavour) into a pale beer. An immersion chiller or a plate chiller gets you to pitching temperature in minutes.
Why a single hop beer teaches the most

A beer with one hop tells you what that hop does. A blend hides it. Comet has a strong personality, so a single hop pale ale is the fastest way to decide whether you like it. Take notes on aroma, bitterness quality and finish. Compare it with a Cascade version if you can.

If you enjoy it, then move to blends. Our guide to resin and bitterness from old hops explains why older varieties can give coarser bitterness, which is worth knowing when you scale up.

Hop oils fade with warmth and air. Freeze the pellets in a sealed bag with the air pressed out. Take out only what you need. A small packet bought for a summer brew and left on a kitchen shelf in Chennai or Bengaluru will smell flat by the time you dry hop. Hop aroma in the finished beer also fades, so drink a hoppy pale ale within a month or two and keep it cold.
Where Comet fits in the bigger picture

Comet is a good example of why old varieties matter. Brewers do not only chase the newest breeding programme. They look for contrast. Our American hops guide maps the older and newer varieties side by side. A Comet beer next to a juicy hazy IPA tastes like a different drink, because the hop is built from different oils.

Read the labels of imported beers and ask a good bottle shop. Look for Comet in single hop series. The more varieties you taste, the more you start to notice the difference between pith and flesh and between resin and fruit. That skill carries into every beer you taste.
faqs: What does Comet hop taste like?
Grapefruit and grapefruit pith with a wild, grassy edge that some people find catty.
It can bitter, with alpha acids around 8 to 11%, but most brewers use it for flavour and aroma.
Can I find Comet in India?
Home brewers usually order hops online from overseas suppliers. Availability and shipping rules change, so check before you plan a brew around it.
